theme: Prayer, fasting, treasure, anxiety, the Father in heaven
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 6:1-34. Jesus turns from the law to the practices of the religious life: giving, praying, and fasting. Then he deals with money and anxiety. Notice how often he says “your Father who sees in secret.”
settingTheScene: The second part of the Sermon is about the heart behind devotion. In first-century Judaism, giving, prayer, and fasting were the three marks of a pious person, and it was tempting to do them for the applause of others. Jesus asks his followers to do them for an audience of one. Then he addresses the two great rivals to trust in the Father: money and worry.
observation: “Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them” (6:1).
“But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (6:3).
“Go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret” (6:6).
“Your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (6:8).
“Pray then like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name” (6:9).
“Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth… but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (6:19-20).
“No one can serve two masters… You cannot serve God and money” (6:24).
“But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (6:33).
interpretation:
Jesus warns about acting religious for show. The people who give, pray, and fast to be seen get exactly what they wanted, the praise of people, and nothing more. Those who do these things in secret have a Father who sees and will reward. The difference is who we are performing for.

At the center is the model prayer. It starts with “Our Father,” not “My Father,” and with God’s name, his kingdom, and his will before our needs. Then it asks for daily bread, forgiveness, and protection from temptation. Notice that the prayer is short and simple. Jesus says that pagans heap up empty phrases, thinking they will be heard for their many words, but the Father already knows what we need. Prayer is not about informing or persuading God. It is about coming to him as children.

The teaching on forgiveness (6:14-15) is sobering. The forgiven are expected to forgive. This is not a transaction, but it describes the character of those who have truly received mercy.

Then Jesus turns to treasure and worry. We cannot serve both God and money. He points to the birds, which do not farm and yet are fed, and to the lilies, which do not spin and yet are clothed. “Are you not of more value than they?” Anxiety assumes that we are on our own. Jesus says we have a Father. The cure for worry is not simply to try harder to stop, but to seek first the kingdom and trust that the Father will provide. Take one day at a time: “Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.”
connection: Isaiah 58:6-9 describes the fasting God desires. Luke 11:1-4 gives Luke’s version of the Lord’s Prayer. 1 Timothy 6:6-10 warns about the love of money. Philippians 4:6-7 says not to be anxious, but to pray with thanksgiving and receive God’s peace. 1 Peter 5:7 says to cast all your anxieties on him because he cares for you. Psalm 55:22 says to cast your burden on the LORD. Romans 8:32 says that the God who gave his Son will also give us all things.
application:
Do one act of giving or service this week that no one will know about except God.

Name your biggest worry. Hand it to the Father in prayer, using Jesus’ reasoning: “You are of more value than the birds.”

Pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly today, pausing on each phrase.
prayerPrompts: Pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly, pausing at each line to add your own words.
Ask him for today’s bread and to forgive your sins.
Ask him to loosen your anxiety and teach you to trust your Father.
